title: Fish Oil and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Triglycerides, Bleeding, Liver
excerpt: Is it safe to take fish oil and drink alcohol? How omega-3 and alcohol affect triglycerides, bleeding risk, heart rhythm, and your liver, and whether fish oil helps a hangover.
metaDescription: Can you take fish oil and drink? How omega-3 and alcohol affect triglycerides, bleeding risk, your liver and hangovers, plus when to talk to a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most healthy adults, taking a normal dose of fish oil and having a few drinks is not a dangerous combination. There is no direct chemical clash between omega-3 fats and alcohol the way there is with some medicines. The real issues are indirect. Alcohol pushes triglycerides (a type of blood fat) up while fish oil is often taken to bring them down, so heavy drinking works against the very reason many people take it. Both fish oil and heavy drinking can make bleeding a little easier, which matters if you take a blood thinner or have surgery coming up. And fish oil does not protect your liver from alcohol or fix a hangover, despite what some wellness posts suggest.

**The quick rules:** Take fish oil with a meal, not on an empty stomach after a night out. Don't count on it to cancel out drinking. If you take fish oil to lower high triglycerides, alcohol is one of the biggest things working against you, so cutting back usually helps more than any capsule. If you take warfarin, apixaban, clopidogrel, daily aspirin, or another blood thinner, or you have a procedure scheduled, tell your doctor about both the fish oil and how much you drink. Avoid cod liver oil if you drink heavily, because it also contains vitamin A, which can add strain on the liver.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before combining fish oil and alcohol if** you take a blood thinner or antiplatelet drug, you take prescription omega-3 (such as Vascepa or Lovaza) for high triglycerides, your triglycerides have ever been above 500 mg/dL, you have had pancreatitis, you have atrial fibrillation or another heart rhythm problem, you have liver disease, or you have surgery or dental work coming up. **Get urgent care** for severe belly pain that spreads to your back (a possible sign of pancreatitis), vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, a racing or irregular heartbeat with chest pain or fainting, or bleeding that won't stop. In an emergency, call 911.

## Is It Safe to Take Fish Oil and Drink Alcohol?

Yes, for most people, at normal doses. Fish oil is a supplement made mostly of two omega-3 fatty acids, **EPA** (eicosapentaenoic acid) and **DHA** (docosahexaenoic acid). Your body treats these as fats. They get absorbed with the rest of the fat in your meal and built into cell membranes over weeks. Alcohol, by contrast, is mainly broken down in the liver by enzymes called alcohol dehydrogenase and CYP2E1. The two don't compete for the same machinery in any meaningful way, so there is no reason to space them hours apart.

That's the reason you won't find an alcohol warning on a typical fish oil bottle, and why major drug-interaction references don't list fish oil and alcohol as a significant interaction for healthy people.

But "no direct interaction" is not the same as "no effect." The questions that actually matter are:

1. **Are you taking fish oil for a reason that alcohol undermines?** For triglycerides, the answer is usually yes.
2. **Do both make bleeding a little easier?** Somewhat, and it matters mostly when other blood-thinning drugs are involved.
3. **Is your liver in good shape?** Fish oil isn't a liver protector, and one type (cod liver oil) adds a separate concern.
4. **How does your stomach feel?** Fish oil can cause reflux and fishy burps, and a stomach irritated by alcohol makes that worse.

The rest of this guide takes each of those in turn.

## Omega-3 and Alcohol: What's Actually Going On in Your Body

It helps to know what each one does to your blood fats, because that's where they meet.

**What fish oil does.** At high doses, EPA and DHA lower triglycerides. They do this mainly by reducing how much triglyceride-rich fat the liver packages up and sends into the bloodstream, and by helping the body clear those fat particles faster. The effect depends heavily on dose. A typical 1,000 mg softgel contains only about 300 mg of actual EPA plus DHA, which is far below the 2 to 4 grams of EPA plus DHA a day used in studies and prescriptions for high triglycerides.

**What alcohol does.** Your liver treats alcohol as a priority. While it's busy breaking down alcohol, it burns less fat for fuel and makes more new fat. Some of that gets stored in the liver itself (the start of fatty liver) and some is exported into the blood as triglycerides. Drinking with a fatty meal adds to the spike. In people who drink regularly, or whose triglycerides are already high, alcohol can raise them a lot.

So the two pull in opposite directions on the same number. A few drinks a week in someone with normal triglycerides isn't much of a tug of war. Several drinks most days in someone taking fish oil to lower a high reading is a tug of war fish oil usually loses.

## Fish Oil, Alcohol, and Triglycerides

This is the most important section if your doctor suggested fish oil because of a blood test.

### Why alcohol matters so much for triglycerides

Among lifestyle factors, alcohol is one of the strongest drivers of high triglycerides. Clinical guidelines for treating high triglycerides, including those from the American Heart Association, list cutting back on alcohol as a first step, alongside reducing sugar and refined carbs, losing excess weight, and being more active. For people with very high levels (500 mg/dL or more), guidelines generally advise avoiding alcohol entirely.

The reason for the stricter rule at very high levels is pancreatitis. When triglycerides get very high, the risk of acute pancreatitis rises, and alcohol is itself a leading cause of pancreatitis. Having both risk factors at once is a combination doctors take seriously.

### Can fish oil "cancel out" drinking?

No. There is no good evidence that taking fish oil offsets the effect of regular drinking on triglycerides. Even at prescription strength, omega-3 lowers triglycerides by a meaningful but limited amount, and the effect is smaller when the underlying driver (like heavy drinking) keeps going. Many people see a bigger drop in triglycerides from cutting back on alcohol than from adding a supplement.

### Over-the-counter vs prescription omega-3

| Type | What it contains | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Standard fish oil softgel | Often about 300 mg EPA + DHA per 1,000 mg capsule | General supplement use; usually too little to move high triglycerides much |
| Concentrated fish oil | Roughly 600 to 900 mg EPA + DHA per capsule, varies by brand | People trying to reach a higher dose with fewer pills |
| Prescription omega-3 (Lovaza and generics) | Concentrated EPA + DHA, typically 4 g a day | Prescribed for very high triglycerides |
| Prescription icosapent ethyl (Vascepa) | Purified EPA only, typically 4 g a day | Prescribed for high triglycerides and, in some patients, to lower heart risk |

If you take a prescription omega-3, you're being treated for a specific problem, and your prescriber should know how much you drink. That conversation is more useful than any general rule in an article. The REDUCE-IT trial, published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 2018, found that icosapent ethyl lowered cardiovascular events in people already on statins who had raised triglycerides. Other large trials of omega-3 products, such as STRENGTH and VITAL, did not show the same benefit, so the picture for heart outcomes depends on the product, the dose, and who is taking it.

If cholesterol is part of your concern too, our guide on [whether alcohol raises cholesterol](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-raise-cholesterol) explains how drinking affects HDL, LDL, and triglycerides separately. If you also take a statin, see [statins and alcohol](/never-hungover/statins-and-alcohol).

## Fish Oil, Alcohol, and Bleeding Risk

Fish oil has a mild blood-thinning effect. Omega-3 fats make platelets (the cells that start a clot) a little less sticky. Heavy drinking also affects clotting: it can lower platelet counts and interfere with how platelets work, and long-term heavy use can damage the liver's ability to make clotting proteins.

How much does this matter in practice?

- **For healthy people at normal doses, not much.** Studies of fish oil at common supplement doses have generally not found a clear rise in serious bleeding. Regulators in the US and Europe have described intakes of up to a few grams of EPA plus DHA a day as safe for most adults.
- **On top of a blood thinner, it's worth a conversation.** Most research has found that fish oil adds little bleeding risk for people on warfarin or antiplatelet drugs at typical doses, but the effect is not zero, and doctors prefer to know. Add regular heavy drinking, which on its own can make warfarin's effect swing up and down, and you have three things nudging bleeding in the same direction.
- **Before surgery or dental work, say something.** Some surgeons ask patients to pause fish oil before a procedure. Practice varies, so follow your own surgeon's advice rather than a general rule. Mention your alcohol use too, because it affects anesthesia and recovery.

Signs that bleeding is becoming a problem include easy or large bruises, nosebleeds that last a long time, bleeding gums, pink or red urine, black or tarry stools, or vomiting blood. The last two need urgent care.

If you take an anticoagulant, our guides on [blood thinners and alcohol](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol) and [warfarin and alcohol](/never-hungover/warfarin-and-alcohol) go into the specific risks.

## Fish Oil and Your Heart Rhythm When You Drink

This is a less-known point that's worth knowing about. Several large trials and later analyses have found that higher-dose omega-3 supplements are linked to a modestly higher risk of **atrial fibrillation**, a common irregular heart rhythm. The link looks strongest at doses above about 1 gram a day.

Alcohol is also a well-known trigger for atrial fibrillation. Episodes after a big night of drinking are common enough that doctors have a nickname for them, "holiday heart."

None of this means a healthy person taking a fish oil capsule should worry about a few drinks. But if you have atrial fibrillation or have been told you're at risk, talk to your doctor about whether high-dose omega-3 makes sense for you, and be honest about your drinking. A racing, fluttering, or irregular heartbeat after drinking deserves a check, and one with chest pain, fainting, or shortness of breath needs urgent care. Our guide on a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers what's normal and what isn't.

## Does Fish Oil Protect Your Liver From Alcohol?

There is no good evidence that fish oil protects the human liver from alcohol damage.

The research here is genuinely mixed:

- **In fatty liver not caused by alcohol**, several clinical trials and reviews have found that omega-3 supplements can lower liver fat somewhat, though they haven't been shown to reverse scarring.
- **In animal studies of alcohol and the liver**, results go both ways. Some studies suggest omega-3 may ease inflammation. A well-known line of older rat research found the opposite: diets rich in fish oil combined with alcohol actually made liver injury worse, likely because polyunsaturated fats are easily oxidized, and alcohol increases oxidative stress in the liver.
- **In people who drink**, there are no solid trials showing fish oil prevents alcohol-related liver disease.

The practical takeaway is that fish oil is not a shield. If you're worried about your liver, the amount you drink matters far more than any supplement.

### A specific warning about cod liver oil

Cod liver oil is not the same as fish oil. Besides omega-3, it contains **vitamin A** and vitamin D, sometimes in large amounts per spoonful. Vitamin A is stored in the liver, and too much can damage it. Regular heavy drinking makes the liver more sensitive to vitamin A toxicity. If you drink heavily, or take other supplements with vitamin A (such as a multivitamin), choose regular fish oil instead and check the label. Our guide to [multivitamins and alcohol](/never-hungover/multivitamin-and-alcohol) covers which vitamins are worth watching when you drink.

## Does Fish Oil Help a Hangover?

There is no good evidence that fish oil prevents or treats a hangover. No meaningful human trials have tested it for this, and its effects (lowering triglycerides, being built into cell membranes over weeks) don't line up with what causes a hangover the next morning.

You'll see two arguments online for taking it:

- **"It fights inflammation."** Hangovers do involve an inflammatory response, and omega-3 has anti-inflammatory effects over the long run. But those effects build up over weeks of steady use. A capsule the night you drink isn't going to change how you feel at 9 a.m.
- **"Alcohol depletes omega-3."** Some animal research suggests chronic heavy drinking can lower DHA levels in the brain and other tissues. That's a reason to eat well if you drink regularly, not evidence that a fish oil pill fixes a hangover.

If anything, fish oil can make a rough morning slightly worse. Its most common side effects are fishy burps, reflux, nausea, and loose stools, and those are more likely on an empty stomach. After drinking, your stomach lining is already irritated. If your gut is unsettled, see our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).

What does help a hangover is less exciting: drinking less and more slowly, eating before and during, alternating with water, and sleeping. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## When to Take Fish Oil If You Drink

Because there's no direct interaction, the timing question is really about comfort and absorption.

- **Take it with a meal that contains some fat.** Omega-3 is absorbed better with food, and you're less likely to get fishy burps.
- **Don't take it on an empty stomach the morning after drinking.** Wait until you've eaten.
- **It doesn't matter much whether you take it on drinking days or not.** Omega-3's effects build over weeks. Missing a day, or taking it at a different time, won't change much. Consistency over time is what counts.
- **Splitting a higher dose between two meals** can help if you get stomach upset.
- **Store it properly.** Fish oil can go rancid. A strong rotten-fish smell when you open a capsule is a sign it has oxidized and should be thrown out.

## How Much Fish Oil Is Reasonable?

These are general figures, not personal advice.

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| General health, healthy adult | Many health bodies suggest eating fatty fish about twice a week; supplements commonly provide 250 to 1,000 mg EPA + DHA a day |
| High triglycerides | Doses of 2 to 4 g EPA + DHA a day are used, usually under a doctor's guidance or by prescription |
| Upper range considered safe for most adults | The FDA has said combined intake of up to 3 g a day of EPA + DHA is generally safe, with no more than 2 g of that from supplements; European regulators have considered up to 5 g a day safe |
| On a blood thinner, before surgery, or with atrial fibrillation | Ask your doctor before starting or raising your dose |

Remember to read the label for the **EPA plus DHA** amount, not the total fish oil amount. A "1,200 mg fish oil" softgel might contain only 360 mg of the omega-3s that matter.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You should talk to your doctor or pharmacist about fish oil and alcohol if you:

- Take a **blood thinner or antiplatelet drug**, including warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, clopidogrel, or daily aspirin
- Take **prescription omega-3** for high triglycerides
- Have **very high triglycerides** or a history of **pancreatitis**
- Have **atrial fibrillation** or another heart rhythm problem
- Have **liver disease** or have been told your liver enzymes are high
- Take **blood pressure medicine**, since fish oil and alcohol can both affect blood pressure
- Have a **fish or shellfish allergy** (some people react to fish oil, though highly refined oils rarely cause problems; ask your allergist)
- Have **surgery or dental work** coming up
- Drink **heavily on a regular basis**, meaning several drinks most days or frequent binges

Bring your full list of medicines and supplements, plus an honest estimate of how much you drink in a typical week. That's what lets them give you a useful answer.

## Fish Oil vs Other Supplements People Take With Alcohol

If you're looking at fish oil because you want to support your body when you drink, here's how it compares with other common choices.

- **Fish oil (omega-3).** Useful for high triglycerides at the right dose, with some heart benefits in specific groups. Not a hangover remedy and not a liver protector.
- **Magnesium.** Heavy drinking can lower magnesium, and some people use it for sleep and muscle cramps. See [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol).
- **Turmeric (curcumin).** Popular for inflammation, with limited human evidence for alcohol-related use. See [turmeric and alcohol](/never-hungover/turmeric-and-alcohol).
- **Milk thistle and NAC.** The two most-studied liver supplements, with mixed human evidence. See [milk thistle and alcohol](/never-hungover/milk-thistle-and-alcohol) and [NAC and alcohol](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol).
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin).** A plant compound studied specifically for alcohol metabolism, covered below.

For a ranked overview with the evidence for each, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## If Your Goal Is Feeling Better After Drinking

Fish oil earns its place for heart and blood-fat reasons, not for the morning after. If what you actually want is to feel better after a night out, the supplement with the most alcohol-specific research is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies on how it affects alcohol metabolism and the liver, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and it doesn't replace drinking less, eating, and hydrating. There's also no evidence it changes how fish oil affects your triglycerides or bleeding risk, so it doesn't change any of the advice above.

There's no known interaction between DHM and fish oil, but if you take a blood thinner or other prescription medicines, check with your pharmacist before adding any new supplement. If you want to try DHM, a well-reviewed premium option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and a budget-friendly one is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) and [dosage calculator](/dhm-dosage-calculator) explain how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Fish oil and alcohol don't interact directly, and a normal dose with a few drinks is fine for most healthy adults.
- Alcohol raises triglycerides, so regular drinking works against one of the main reasons people take fish oil. Cutting back often helps more than the capsule.
- Fish oil and heavy drinking both affect clotting. If you take a blood thinner or have surgery coming up, tell your doctor about both.
- Higher-dose omega-3 and alcohol can each raise the chance of atrial fibrillation. If you have a rhythm problem, talk to your doctor.
- There is no good evidence that fish oil protects your liver from alcohol or helps a hangover. Skip cod liver oil if you drink heavily.
- Take fish oil with a meal, not on an empty stomach the morning after.

For how fish oil fits with other supplements people take around drinking, see our overview of [the vitamins and minerals alcohol depletes](/never-hungover/vitamins-depleted-by-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take fish oil and drink alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no direct interaction between omega-3 fats and alcohol, so a normal dose of fish oil and a few drinks is not a dangerous combination. The main concerns are indirect: alcohol raises triglycerides (which fish oil is often taken to lower), both can make bleeding slightly easier, and fish oil can upset a stomach already irritated by drinking. Talk to your doctor if you take a blood thinner, prescription omega-3, or have liver or heart rhythm problems.

**Does alcohol cancel out fish oil?**

Not exactly, but regular drinking works against it. Alcohol prompts the liver to make and release more triglycerides, while fish oil helps lower them. If you take fish oil for high triglycerides and drink regularly, the alcohol can blunt or outweigh the benefit. For many people, cutting back on alcohol lowers triglycerides more than adding a supplement does.

**Should I take omega-3 before or after drinking?**

It doesn't make much difference. Omega-3's effects build up over weeks of steady use, so timing on a single day matters little. The best approach is to take it with a meal that contains some fat, which improves absorption and reduces fishy burps. Avoid taking it on an empty stomach the morning after drinking, when your stomach is already irritated.

**Does fish oil help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that fish oil prevents or treats a hangover. It hasn't been properly tested for this in people, and its anti-inflammatory effects build slowly over weeks rather than overnight. It can even make a queasy morning a little worse, since nausea, reflux, and loose stools are common side effects. Drinking less, eating, hydrating, and sleeping are what actually help.

**Is it safe to take fish oil and alcohol with blood thinners?**

Check with your doctor. Fish oil has a mild blood-thinning effect, and heavy drinking can affect platelets and make warfarin levels unstable. Most research suggests fish oil adds little bleeding risk at typical doses for people on blood thinners, but the effects can add up, and doctors want to know about all three. Get urgent care for black or tarry stools, vomiting blood, or bleeding that won't stop.

**Does fish oil protect your liver from alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that it does. Omega-3 has been shown in some trials to reduce liver fat in fatty liver disease not caused by alcohol, but there are no solid human trials showing it prevents alcohol-related liver damage. Some older animal studies even found that fish oil combined with alcohol made liver injury worse. The amount you drink matters far more for your liver than any supplement.

**Is cod liver oil safe if you drink?**

Be more careful with cod liver oil than regular fish oil. Cod liver oil contains vitamin A, which is stored in the liver and can harm it in high amounts, and regular heavy drinking makes the liver more sensitive to vitamin A. If you drink heavily or take other vitamin A supplements, choose a standard fish oil and check the label.

**Can fish oil and alcohol cause an irregular heartbeat?**

They can each raise the risk in some people. Studies have linked higher-dose omega-3 supplements, especially above about 1 gram a day, to a modestly higher chance of atrial fibrillation, and heavy drinking is a well-known trigger for it. A healthy person taking a standard capsule shouldn't worry about a few drinks, but if you have atrial fibrillation or notice a racing or irregular heartbeat after drinking, talk to your doctor. Chest pain, fainting, or shortness of breath needs urgent care.
